name: Thangka
description: Painted or embroidered scroll of Buddhist deities and mandalas, framed in silk and hung in Tibetan Buddhist monasteries and homes of the Himalayan world. Thangkas are painted with mineral pigments to exact iconographic rule, and the images are regarded as aids to meditation and carriers of the blessing of the figures they depict.
material: cotton or silk, mineral pigments, gold

name: Singing Bowl
description: Metal bowl that rings a sustained tone when its rim is rubbed with a wooden striker, used in Himalayan Buddhist ritual for offerings and meditation. The bowls are held to clear and focus the mind, and their sound is used to open and close ceremonies in the monasteries of Nepal and Tibet, where the ringing is read as an offering to the deities.
source: Himalayan ritual practice and craft tradition

name: Dorje
description: Ritual thunderbolt of Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhism, a bronze sceptre with five-pronged ends that stands for the indestructible method of enlightenment. Vajra in Sanskrit, the dorje is paired with the ritual bell in monastic hand rituals and echoes the old thunder-weapon of the gods in Himalayan ritual art, where it is held by monks during ceremonies.

name: Drilbu Bell
description: Ritual hand bell of Himalayan Buddhism, struck and rung during ceremonies and paired with the dorje sceptre, cast in an alloy that rings with a long clear note. The drilbu's sound is held to summon compassion and mark the moments of a ritual, and its handle carries the face of a deity, most often Prajnaparamita, the goddess of wisdom.

name: Khomus (Yakut Jew's Harp)
description: Metal Jew's harp of the Yakut (Sakha) people, an elongated iron frame with a flexible steel tongue, played by plucking the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The khomus imitates bird calls and natural sounds, accompanied songs and held shamanic associations. Yakutsk's Khomus Museum, the republic's Khomus Day and an international festival honour it as a symbol of Sakha culture.
material: iron or steel frame and tongue
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Khomus'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Khomus Museum, Yakutsk

name: Serge (Yakut Carved Hitching Post)
description: Carved wooden hitching post of the Yakut (Sakha) people, set up at home and at the ysyakh summer festival, often topped with carved horse-heads. The sacred Aar Baah Serge of the festival stands on the eastern side as a symbolic world-tree, a ladder linking earth to the upper world where the aiyy deities dwell; horses are tied facing east during the celebration.
source: Gogolev et al., 'Yakut National Holiday — Ysyakh: traditions and modernity' (Berghahn Books)

name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)
description: Traditional knife of the Yakut (Sakha) people, with an asymmetric blade bearing a fuller on one side and a convex edge on the other, a birch-burl handle and a leather sheath. Forged by Yakut blacksmiths from local iron since pre-Russian times, it is used for carving wood, dressing hides and preparing fish and meat — an everyday tool with a remarkably constant design.
material: locally smelted iron, birch burl handle, leather sheath
era: ancient; similar knives found in Yakut burial grounds
source: Wikipedia 'Yakutian knife'; ar.culture.ru 'Yakutian knife'; Russian Museum of Ethnography

name: Choron (Yakut Kumys Vessel)
description: Carved wooden drinking vessel of the Yakut (Sakha) people, made from a single piece of birch or spruce burl, with a conical or rounded body and short legs. The choron is the principal ritual vessel of the ysyakh summer festival, filled with kumys and offered in honour of the aiyy deities, then shared among the celebrants; its elegant form is held to resemble a bird.

name: Buryat Shaman's Drum (Hese)
description: Oval single-headed frame drum of the Buryat shaman (bo), fitted with a cross-shaped handle and a rawhide head often painted with images of animals and the world tree. Struck to summon spirits and to carry the shaman between the worlds, the drum (hese) is the central instrument of Buryat ritual practice; obtaining one marked the shaman's consecration.
material: wooden frame, rawhide head, iron handle
source: Wierucka, 'Shamanism in the Baikal Region' (2013); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat drum'

name: Buryat Shaman's Horse-Staff
description: Ritual staff of the Buryat shaman, carved from birch wood and topped with a horse's head; senior shamans who had passed the fifth consecration carried iron-tipped versions. In Buryat belief the horse-staff served as the shaman's mount to ride through the spirit world, and it remains a recognised emblem of Buryat shamanic practice alongside the drum.
source: Czaplicka, 'Shamanism in Siberia' (1914); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat shaman's staff'

name: Igil (Tuvan Horsehead Fiddle)
description: Two-stringed bowed fiddle of the Tuvans, its hollow wooden body covered with hide and its neck crowned with a carved horse's head. The igil accompanies khoomei throat singing and Tuvan epic song, evoking the gait and voice of a steppe horse; it is prized across Central Asia and appears in the collection of the Russian Museum of Ethnography.
material: wooden body, hide soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Alash Ensemble; ar.culture.ru 'Igil'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Doshpuluur (Tuvan Three-String Lute)
description: Long-necked, three-stringed plucked lute of the Tuvans, with a small wooden body often carved in a canoe shape and gut or nylon strings. The doshpuluur forms a key part of Tuvan music, accompanying songs and dance and often played in duet with the igil; it is a close relative of the Altai topshur and Mongolian tovshuur.

name: Topshur (Altai Two-String Lute)
description: Two-stringed plucked lute of the Altai people, carved with a shallow bowl body, hide soundboard and gut or horsehair strings. The topshur accompanies the kaychi storytellers, who perform the great Altai heroic epics such as the Tale of Maadai-Kara; its music is bound to Altai oral tradition and is often played before the fire and during ritual.
material: wood body, hide soundboard, gut/horsehair strings

name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
description: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut khomus and Buryat khuur.
material: iron, brass or wood; steel tongue
source: ar.culture.ru 'Komus (Altai)'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Evenki Shaman's Costume
description: Ceremonial cloak of the Evenki shaman, sewn from reindeer hide and hung with iron pendants shaped as birds, fish, deer, snakes and human figures that represent the shaman's spirit-helpers, with a fringed apron and iron rattles. The costume is preserved in the collections of the Russian Museum of Ethnography and Siberian regional museums.
material: reindeer hide (rovduga), iron pendants, leather fringe
source: ar.culture.ru 'Evenk shaman costume'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Nivkh Shaman's Drum
description: Oval frame drum of the Nivkh people of Sakhalin and the Amur region, with a wooden handle, used by the shaman to accompany spirit journeys and healing rituals. Its sound marks the shaman's passage between the worlds, as recorded by ethnographers including Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney in her study of Nivkh shamanism.
material: wooden frame, hide head, wooden handle
